This review highlights a concerning thing, which I didn't see anywhere before: The Start Menu can only hold up to 500 items, after which the menu database stops accepting more. This, to me, indicates that:

  1. When a program is uninstalled and the database drops below 500 items, the next available program will not get included in the Start Menu, as there is no queue (this was also mentioned in the article).
  2. Third-party shells, like Classic Shell may face the same issue, as they'd reference the same database.

500 items isn't so much. The default installation of PDFCreator places 11 shortcuts in the Start Menu, PuTTY places 6, DOSBox has 10, and those are only small programs. I'm easily way over 1000 items on my home desktop - the Start Menu is three columns wide and in some places up to five sub-folders deep. Until this is resolved, I won't even look at Win10.

The items are sorted like the old menu system if it is related to the program, then a drop down is added, this a mis-representation of what is meant my max of 500 so your argument is a non issue in this case.

For Example: PDFCreator would only occupy 1 slot the 10 would under the drop down. So you could install 500 programs yet have 10 or more links per slot in the drop down. If you have 500 individually wrapped programs installed, it's time for a tidy up or to re-think your life goals. :)

If you have 500 individually wrapped programs installed, it's time for a tidy up or to re-think your life goals.

While I agree 500 programs is probably a bit much, there's absolutely no reason for a restriction like this.
Memory usage, registry size, CPU usage on load. There are a lot of reasons, mainly performance based. Although I do agree, the restriction should be user choice if the need arises.

If parsing more than 500 items causes such significant performance issues, there's an underlying flaw in their algorithm. Modern databases contain vastly higher order of magnitudes of entries. At most, the start menu should only parse the first 500 items and have an option to display the rest. There is no reason for a soft cap on how many programs we can have installed and registered through the start menu.

I see no reason why parsing entries for the start menu would run in anything besides O(n) time (edit:) to load all n programs.

I have over 200 programs installed on Windows 10 and am only using 285 positions on the start menu, recent menu and metro menu combined. I think anyone with 500+ entries on the start menu has too much stuff installed. But it will most likely be increased....if it hasn't already.
